AI Startup Plaud Plans to File for U.S. IPO in 2028 — Interview
By Kimberley Kao
AI startup Plaud plans to file for a U.S. initial public offering in 2028, according to co-founder and Chief Executive Nathan Xu.

The San Francisco-based company will be ready for an IPO once annual revenue exceeds $1 billion, Xu said in an interview. Plaud is targeting $500 million in global sales this year as it continues to grow rapidly.
The company recently said it reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue within two years and now serves more than 2.5 million users across over 170 countries. Plaud was incorporated in 2022.
Plaud designs AI-powered note-taking devices and software. One of its products, the Plaud Note, attaches to a smartphone and can record, transcribe and summarize phone conversations.

"I find it always difficult to keep track of all the best ideas and also the details, which causes a lot of pain [when] you feel that you are not able to catch up," said Xu, an experience that inspired him to create the company.
Xu said the company was valued at over $1 billion dollars as of last year and is currently "highly profitable."
Venture-capital firm Vertex Holdings is currently Plaud's largest investor, according to Xu.

Vertex Holdings, a wholly owned subsidiary of Singapore state-investment firm Temasek Holdings, operates a global network of funds under the Vertex Ventures name. Vertex was an early investor in Chinese robotics company Unitree and Southeast Asian technology company Grab.
Plaud sources chips from external companies, including Taiwanese semiconductor firm Realtek, and assembles its products in Shenzhen, China. It designs and engineers its devices in-house, Xu said.

Plaud has about 300 employees in China and around 100 in San Francisco, as well as operations in Europe, Japan and Southeast Asia. The U.S. and Europe markets account for about two-thirds of the business, Xu said.
Plaud on Wednesday announced the opening of its new Asia-Pacific headquarters in Singapore, where its headcount has grown to 100 staff from 10 in nine months.
As Plaud expands, Xu said a key priority is securing the "best talent." That objective is also shaping its acquisition strategy.

Plaud is primarily interested in acquiring companies with strong talent that could help it develop capabilities it can't build quickly enough on its own, rather than adding new users or products, he said.
Xu said Plaud had explored acquisitions, but none had succeeded.
Rapid technological change is also forcing the company to make tough choices about where to invest.
"It's something very difficult to navigate...[there are] too many changes and too many choices and you get to bet what you think would be right for the next 12 months," Xu said.
